claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, metastable solid solution.
At service-relevant temperatures, the metastable solid solution transforms through a discontinuous, diffusion-controlled precipitation reaction.
The precipitation reaction produces Mg-rich intermetallic compounds by nucleation and growth.
Mg-rich intermetallic formation disrupts the uniformity of the protective oxide associated with the metastable state.
Disruption of the protective oxide reduces both corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Annealing at approximately 600–800°C will promote intermetallic nucleation and growth relative to rapid cooling that retains the metastable solid solution.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates form both at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Local diffusion of Mg at elevated temperature triggers discontinuous precipitation.
The precipitates create compositional heterogeneity and non-uniform interfaces.
Compositional heterogeneity and non-uniform interfaces hinder formation of a continuous protective oxide layer.
Annealed samples will contain significantly more well-distributed intermetallic precipitates than the initial metastable state.
Annealed samples will exhibit decreased corrosion resistance, reflected by higher corrosion-current density or more negative corrosion potential.
Annealed samples will exhibit poorer high-temperature oxidation performance, reflected by higher oxidation rates or less-protective oxide scales.
The as-cast or as-quenched metastable solid-solution state has enhanced passivation and effective corrosion and oxidation resistance.
The proposed mechanism is applicable in service regimes near 600–800°C under environments that challenge protective-oxide integrity.
The proposed behavior may not apply outside the specified thermal and chemical exposure window.
